stories.title: Prosper and Versluys Close $50M Land Deal for $650M Miami Condo Tower
stories.excerpt: Prosper Group and Versluys Group have paid $50 million for a development site in Miami’s Brickell district, where they plan to build a $650 million condo tower, the joint venture announced. The 1-acre assemblage includes three parcels: one along the Miami River, with more than 300 feet of water frontage, as well as two adjacent inland spots at 66 Southwest Sixth Street and 625 Southwest First Avenue, near the Brickell City Center mixed-use complex. The joint venture plans to develop a 60-story waterfront high-rise with 181 condos. Vaster provided a $30.5 million loan for the acquisition, which has been under contract for at least eight months. The sellers, developers Two Roads Development and Newgard Development Group, are currently building another luxury complex on a neighboring lot at 99 Southwest Seventh Street. Last year, the joint venture nabbed a $513 million financing package for the construction of two condo towers: a 46-story, 422-unit building branded after the Standard Hotel and the 44-stories, 362-unit Lofty Brickell building. The Brickell project marks the first U.S. endeavor for Belgian developer Versluys Group, which was founded in 1908. Prosper, led and founded by former Wall Street financier Jay Roberts, has made inroads in Miami real estate in recent years, though no projects have reached the construction phase yet. Brickell is seeing a rush of luxury development. Along the bayfront, billionaire hedge funder Ken Griffin is planning to build a mixed-use complex, including a 54-story office skyscraper. The Cipriani-branded and St Regis-branded condo projects remain under construction. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Prosper & Versluys pay $50M for 1-acre Brickell Miami assemblage; plan $650M 60-story condo tower
Vaster provides $30.5M acquisition loan; JV secured $513M construction financing last year for two towers
Waterfront Miami Brickell sees continued luxury condo development capital flowing to scarce infill sites
stories.summary: Prosper Group and Versluys Group acquired a three-parcel, 1-acre assemblage in Miami's Brickell district for $50 million, planning a 60-story, 181-unit luxury condo tower with 300+ feet of Miami River frontage. Vaster Bank provided the $30.5 million acquisition loan. The joint venture already secured a $513 million construction financing package last year for two additional towers (46-story, 422 units and another project). This marks continued investor appetite for waterfront mixed-use and condo development in Miami's core urban district.
stories.impact: Miami Brickell demand remains robust for luxury residential; waterfront scarcity and entitlements attract institutional capital, supporting land valuations and enabling larger mixed-use/condo pipelines. However, this is condos, not rentals—less direct relevance to multifamily development, though signals strong Miami metro absorption and pricing power that anchors overall residential market strength.

stories.title: Hawkins Way, Varde Acquire East Village Student Housing
stories.excerpt: Hawkins Way Capital and joint venture partner Varde Partners completed the acquisition of 81 E. 3rd St., a student housing property located in Manhattan’s East Village. Acquired for $28 million, the off-market transaction marks a strategic addition to the growing FOUND Study student housing portfolio and expands the platform’s presence in one of New York City’s most sought-after neighborhoods. The property features apartment-style layouts that offer an enhanced living experience, compared to traditional dormitory accommodations, according to Hawkins Way. Its flexible design also provides long-term optionality, with the ability to serve both student housing and conventional multifamily uses. “The East Village has long been a market we have targeted, given its concentration of students, proximity to leading universities, and enduring real estate fundamentals,” said Ross Walker, Managing Partner, Hawkins Way. “This acquisition expands our JV’s presence in one of Manhattan’s most dynamic neighborhoods and reinforces our strategy of investing in well-located urban student housing assets positioned to benefit from sustained demand.” The post Hawkins Way, Varde Acquire East Village Student Housing appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hawkins Way & Varde acquire 81 E. 3rd St. East Village for $28M off-market; expand FOUND Study platform
Student housing asset with apartment-style layouts; flexible conversion to conventional multifamily optionality
Manhattan East Village targeted for sustained student concentration, proximity to universities, proven fundamentals
stories.summary: Hawkins Way Capital and Varde Partners completed a $28 million off-market acquisition of 81 E. 3rd St., a student housing property in Manhattan's East Village. The asset features apartment-style layouts and offers long-term flexibility to serve both student housing and conventional multifamily uses. The acquisition expands the FOUND Study platform's presence in a neighborhood with high student density and proximity to leading universities.
stories.impact: Manhattan East Village student housing remains a stable, in-demand niche with inherent conversion optionality; acquisition signals confidence in sustained NYU and New School enrollment and captures durable demand in one of the city's tightest submarkets. Flexible-use design de-risks regulatory or demographic shifts that could pressure student housing, making this attractive for yield-focused investors in a high-barrier-to-entry submarket.

stories.title: Former Blue Shield of CA Offices Trade for Residential Conversion
stories.excerpt: NAI Capital Commercial executive managing director Ryan Campbell, SIOR, represented The Olson Company in its $24,850,000 acquisition of a 7.9-acre office campus at 601 Potrero Grande Dr. and 2100 Saturn St. in Monterey Park. The campus includes two office buildings totaling 120,191 square feet. The buyer plans to redevelop the property into a new residential community. Originally built in 1980, the campus was previously owned and occupied by Blue Shield of California. Andrew Harper, Jeff Bramson, and Will Poulsen of JLL represented the seller. “This acquisition reflects the continued shift toward repositioning well-located office properties into much-needed housing throughout the San Gabriel Valley,” said Campbell. “Large infill redevelopment opportunities like this are increasingly rare. The size, location, and long-term potential of this campus make it exceptionally well-suited to deliver new housing while transforming an underutilized office property into a vibrant residential community.” The post Former Blue Shield of CA Offices Trade for Residential Conversion appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Olson Company buys 7.9-acre former Blue Shield office campus for $24.85M in Monterey Park
120,191 sq ft, two buildings (built 1980); planned conversion to new residential community
San Gabriel Valley office-to-residential conversion reflects regional housing demand and office obsolescence
stories.summary: The Olson Company acquired a 7.9-acre office campus (601 Potrero Grande Drive and 2100 Saturn Street) in Monterey Park for $24.85 million, formerly occupied by Blue Shield of California since 1980. The 120,191-square-foot, two-building property is slated for redevelopment into a residential community. The acquisition exemplifies the broader trend of office repositioning into housing throughout the San Gabriel Valley.
stories.impact: San Gabriel Valley office-to-residential conversions signal sustained housing demand and the economic viability of adaptive reuse in infill markets; low acquisition cost ($207/sq ft) and large footprint suggest strong residential economics and weak office fundamentals. This is a leading indicator of entitled conversion opportunities in the LA subregion—developers should scout additional underutilized office campuses where zoning/entitlements already permit or facilitate residential use.

stories.title: JAMS Relocating New York Offices to 3 Times Square
stories.excerpt: Rudin has secured an agreement with JAMS, a provider of alternative dispute resolution services, to relocate its New York Resolution Center to 3 Times Square. The tenant will occupy 55,335 square feet across the entirety of the building’s top two floors. As part of the 11-year lease, JAMS is expected to move from its current offices at 620 Eighth Ave. in the fourth quarter of 2027. “JAMS’ major commitment to 3 Times Square underscores the market’s continued appetite for top-quality, well-located properties with premier amenity programs,” said Michael Rudin, co-CEO of Rudin. “JAMS joins a diverse roster of high-caliber companies who value vibrant, transit-connected Midtown Manhattan office destinations.” Rudin was represented in-house by Kevin Daly along with the Cushman & Wakefield team of Ron LoRusso, Lou D’Avanzo, John Cefaly, Michael Burgio, Dan Organ and Paige Engeldrum. Ken Rapp, Brendan Herlihy and Ron Wade of CBRE represented JAMS. The post JAMS Relocating New York Offices to 3 Times Square appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: JAMS leases 55,335 sq ft across top two floors of 3 Times Square; 11-year term, move Q4 2027
Relocation from 620 Eighth Ave; signals Rudin's market confidence and Midtown office tenant stickiness
Return-to-office momentum in premium, transit-connected Midtown Manhattan buildings with amenity programming
stories.summary: Rudin Management secured an 11-year lease with JAMS (alternative dispute resolution services) for 55,335 square feet spanning the top two floors of 3 Times Square. JAMS will relocate from its current offices at 620 Eighth Avenue in Q4 2027. The deal underscores ongoing tenant appetite for high-quality, well-located Midtown Manhattan office space with premium amenities.
stories.impact: Strong office leasing in prime Midtown Manhattan—especially trophy assets with transit access and modern amenities—attracts and retains quality tenants and stabilizes office valuations; however, this does not directly affect multifamily supply or demand. Indirectly, it signals corporate employment stability and wage growth in NYC, which supports residential demand and rent growth across the metro.

stories.title: Shopoff Sells Site of Proposed Newport Beach Condo Development
stories.excerpt: Shopoff Realty Investments has sold a proposed 1.06-acre condominium development, Park Palm in Newport Beach, to Shea Homes for an undisclosed sum. The property is part of Shopoff’s master plan community, Uptown Newport Village, and is entitled for 23 townhomes. Shopoff acquired the 25-acre Uptown Newport Village site in December 2010. The firm set out to repurpose the land for a mixed-use residential village, rather than maintain its prior office and industrial uses. In 2013, Shopoff completed the entitlement process, allowing for master development to include 1,244 residential units, 11,500 square feet of commercial/retail space and two one-acre parks. Phase I of the project has seen multiple developments completed, beginning with One Uptown Newport in 2019. Park Palm, which has been entitled for 23 townhomes, will round out Phase I. Construction on Park Palm is anticipated to begin in 2027, with completion expected in 2028-2029. The post Shopoff Sells Site of Proposed Newport Beach Condo Development appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Shopoff sells Park Palm (1.06-acre, 23-unit townhome site) to Shea Homes; part of Uptown Newport Village
Master plan entitled for 1,244 units total; Phase I nearing completion, Phase II (Park Palm) construction 2027–2029
Newport Beach mixed-use village conversion from office/industrial reflects OC residential demand and long entitlement timeline
stories.summary: Shopoff Realty Investments sold Park Palm, a 1.06-acre condominium development site in Newport Beach, to Shea Homes (undisclosed price). The property is part of Shopoff's 25-acre Uptown Newport Village master plan, entitled in 2013 for 1,244 residential units, 11,500 sq ft of retail, and two parks. Park Palm is entitled for 23 townhomes with construction expected 2027–2029. Phase I began deliveries in 2019.
stories.impact: Long-duration, large-footprint mixed-use village projects in OC infill (office-to-residential repurposing) take 10+ years from acquisition to final phase—illustrating extended capital lock-up, entitlement complexity, and phased absorption risk. However, successful Phase I execution and off-loading to a major builder (Shea) de-risks Phase II and signals durable OC residential demand; developers should monitor absorption pace and pricing to gauge broader OC multifamily market health.

stories.title: JLL Lists Staten Island Waterfront Development for $45M
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets has been retained by Traingle Equities as sales advisor for Lighthouse Point, a newly completed, transit-oriented, Class A multifamily waterfront development located at 5 Bay St. in the St. George neighborhood of Staten Island. The asking price is $45 million. Lighthouse Point is a mixed-use development situated adjacent to the Staten Island Ferry Terminal. Occupying the site of the historic U.S. Lighthouse Service’s General Depot, the recently completed first phase features 115 residential units. The JLL Capital Markets Investment Sales and Advisory team representing the seller is led by Senior Managing Directors Rob Hinckley and Jeff Julien, Managing Director Steven Rutman and Director Devon Warren. “Lighthouse Point presents a rare opportunity in today’s market,” said Warren. “It’s a well-conceived project in a market where new development opportunities are increasingly limited, and we think buyers will recognize both the quality of what’s been built and the potential that’s still ahead.” The post JLL Lists Staten Island Waterfront Development for $45M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Triangle Equities lists Lighthouse Point (Staten Island Ferry-adjacent, 115-unit Class A, mixed-use) for $45M
Recently completed Phase 1; transit-oriented waterfront development on historic U.S. Lighthouse Service depot site
Staten Island waterfront Class A multifamily with ferry access and future phase optionality attracts institutional capital
stories.summary: JLL Capital Markets is marketing Lighthouse Point, a newly completed, Class A, transit-oriented waterfront multifamily development at 5 Bay Street in Staten Island's St. George neighborhood, for $45 million. Phase 1 features 115 residential units in a mixed-use property adjacent to the Staten Island Ferry Terminal on the historic U.S. Lighthouse Service General Depot site. Additional phases are envisioned.
stories.impact: Staten Island waterfront developments with ferry transit access and Class A amenities command institutional buyer interest and signal market recognition of Staten Island as an underserved, accessible outer-borough residential destination; strong $45M ask on 115 units (~$391K/unit) indicates pricing power. Developers should evaluate other Staten Island ferry-proximate infill sites for similar transit-anchored, mixed-use plays—supply is constrained, and NYC metro rental demand remains robust.

stories.title: Brookfield Asset Management Raises Record $77B in Q2
stories.excerpt: Brookfield Asset Management raised a record $77 billion in the second quarter of 2026, bringing its assets under management to more than $1 trillion, the investment firm reported in an earnings call Wednesday. Year-to-date, the investor has brought in $98 billion, more than half of what Brookfield raised for all last year. It also deployed $21 billion this past quarter. Brookfield’s seventh flagship private equity fund raised $6.7 billion during the quarter, while its sixth flagship infrastructure fund brought in $9.3 billion, putting both on pace to become the largest funds of their respective vintages. The firm also secured $5 billion in commitments for its first AI Infrastructure Fund. In another AI-focused venture, Brookfield increased its financing framework with Bloom Energy for AI infrastructure power projects to $25 billion, up from the $5 billion commitment announced in October 2025. “We can source and entitle power land, develop and operate large-scale AI factories, deliver behind-the-meter and baseload power, provide contracted compute, and pursue partnerships with some of the major stakeholders, including semiconductor players and hyperscalers,” said Sikander Rashid, Brookfield’s global head of AI infrastructure. “Not many firms can bring all of that together.” On the real estate front, Brookfield also raised $4.3 billion across segment funds and deployed $5.2 billion, buying a privately held U.S. manufactured-home portfolio and the taking private of an outdoor industrial storage portfolio. Brookfield also completed its purchase of Oaktree, buying the remaining 26 percent stake for about $3 billion. The move is meant to bolster Brookfield’s credit business. “We really see the upside for that business is on the revenue front, the ability to include Oaktree into Brookfield’s broader distribution, product development, multi-asset programs with our largest partners,” said Brookfield CEO Connor Teskey, who assumed the position in February. bullets: Brookfield raises record $77B in Q2 2026; AUM exceeds $1T; $98B year-to-date (2026)
Flagship PE Fund VII raised $6.7B, Infrastructure Fund VI raised $9.3B; $5B committed to first AI Infrastructure Fund

The firm deployed $21 billion last quarter, with flagship PE Fund VII raising $6.7 billion and Infrastructure Fund VI raising $9.3 billion. Brookfield also secured $5 billion commitments for its first AI Infrastructure Fund and increased its Bloom Energy partnership framework to $25 billion for AI power infrastructure.
stories.impact: Massive capital availability for infrastructure, PE, and AI-powered projects signals strong institutional investor appetite and potential for increased land acquisition and development financing across sectors. However, AI infrastructure capital is competing for land, power, and financing—developers should monitor whether rising AI infrastructure capex and land scarcity drive up cost inputs (labor, materials, entitlements) in major metros, potentially reducing multifamily development ROI.

stories.title: Return-to-Office Gained New Momentum in First Half of 2026: Report
stories.excerpt: U.S. office attendance is on the rise, but the return-to-office trend remains a tale of two cities. In the first half of 2026, office visits nationwide rose 6 percent year-over-year, and achieved the narrowest first-half gap from pre-pandemic levels thus far, data from foot-traffic tracker Placer.ai shows. The six-month period of foot traffic marked acceleration from the 1.9 percent annual uptick observed in the same period of 2025. Office attendance is far from a full and even recovery, however. U.S. office visits remain 31.2 percent below 2019 levels, according to Placer.ai’s August office market report. While Miami and New York are making strides toward baseline visitation levels, Denver and Chicago still have a long way to go. The hybrid workweek also appears here to stay –– for now. The report’s survey of 11 major U.S. markets revealed that office attendance diverges widely across geographies. Cubicles and corner offices are filling up in Miami, where attendance in the first half of the year was 11.5 percent below that of 2019. First-half attendance in Denver, on the other hand, remained more than 40 percent below 2019 levels. The “most improved” award for the period of January through June goes to West Coast hubs Los Angeles and San Francisco, with annual visitation upticks of 13 percent and 10.9 percent, respectively. The pair of cities achieved the report’s largest year-over-year gains. Hybrid workweeks have made a lasting impact on U.S. corporate culture, but the model’s popularity is waning in some markets. The country’s highest shares of Friday office attendance belong to Miami and Dallas, where roughly one in seven weekday office visits fell on a Friday. In Chicago, however, Fridays account for less than one out of every 10 office visits. This is the same city where personalized video platform Cameo announced last year a $10,000 raise for every new and existing employee that returns to its Fulton Market office four days per week. bullets: U.S. office attendance rose 6% YoY in H1 2026; remains 31.2% below 2019 levels nationwide
Miami office visits 11.5% below 2019; Denver and Chicago still 40%+ below pre-pandemic; hybrid workweek persists
Return-to-office trend remains geographically fragmented; limited office demand recovery limits office-to-multifamily conversion urgency
stories.summary: U.S. office attendance rose 6 percent year-over-year in the first half of 2026, accelerating from the 1.9 percent uptick in H1 2025, but overall visits remain 31.2 percent below 2019 baseline levels. Miami and New York show strong recovery momentum, while Denver and Chicago remain 40+ percent below pre-pandemic levels. Placer.ai data indicates hybrid work is enduring and recovery is highly geography-dependent.
stories.impact: Office recovery remains weak and uneven across metros; Miami and NYC multifamily benefits from some return-to-office tailwinds, but Denver and Chicago office-to-residential conversions may face slower demand absorption due to ongoing hybrid/remote work. Developers in weak RTO markets should prioritize conversions only if supported by direct residential demand fundamentals (population growth, job creation outside office sector), not office recovery assumptions.

stories.title: Krea USA Nabs $62M Construction Loan for Lauderhill, Fla., Rental
stories.excerpt: Krea USA nabbed a $61.8 million construction loan for a multifamily development in Lauderhill, Fla., property records show. The financing from Abanca Bank covers the 385-unit Le Parc at Lauderhill development, at 3831 Northwest 13th Street, just east of the Lauderhill Mall and North State Road 7. The 10-acre development will include three eight-story buildings, including a day care operated by a nonprofit and no other commercial space on the ground floor. Construction started in March and is expected to be completed next year. The project has undergone a few changes since first being pitched in 2020. It was originally envisioned as a workforce housing development, with Vivian Dimond’s Bayshore Capital Grove as a partner. Fast forward six years, the development will have no rental restrictions, and Krea USA bought out Bayshore Capital Grove’s stake, Akrisht Pandey, Krea USA’s director of real estate, told Commercial Observer. Still, a tax abatement amounting to $9.1 million over 10 years, which the City of Lauderhill approved in 2022, will remain, Pandey added. Rents are expected to range between 100 and 120 percent of the area’s median income. The developer will build a public road. Krea USA, led by founder and CEO Mauricio Girault, specializes in mixed-income multifamily residential properties. In January, the Miami-based firm proposed building an affordable homeownership condominium in Miami’s Overtown neighborhood on land owned by the city, the South Florida Business Journal reported. A representative for Bayshore Capital Grove did not respond to requests for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Krea USA secures $61.8M construction loan (Abanca Bank) for Le Parc at Lauderhill; 385 units, 10-acre site
Three eight-story buildings; construction started March 2025, completion expected 2026; $9.1M tax abatement (10-year)
Originally workforce housing, now market-rate; Krea bought out Bayshore Capital Grove; Lauderhill submarket sees consistent rental development
stories.summary: Krea USA obtained a $61.8 million construction loan from Abanca Bank for Le Parc at Lauderhill, a 385-unit, 10-acre multifamily development in Lauderhill, Florida, just east of Lauderhill Mall. The project comprises three eight-story buildings and a nonprofit day care. Construction started in March 2025 and is expected to complete in 2026. The project has pivoted from workforce housing (workforce rental restrictions) to unrestricted market-rate, with Krea USA buying out original partner Bayshore Capital Grove. A $9.1 million, 10-year City of Lauderhill tax abatement remains in place.
stories.impact: South Florida (Lauderhill/Broward submarket) multifamily construction financing remains readily available; conversion from workforce to market-rate reflects confidence in unsubsidized rent growth and broader South Florida rental demand strength. Tax abatements continue to sweeten development economics—developers should monitor Broward County and neighboring metros for similar PILOT/abatement programs that enhance feasibility in secondary markets.

stories.title: In Largest U.S. Multifamily Sale Since 2024, BlackRock Pays $1.63B in SoCal
stories.excerpt: BlackRock has acquired more than 3,600 rental residential units in Southern California in one of the region’s largest commercial real estate deals in recent memory. It’s also the largest U.S. multifamily sale since June 2024. One of the investment vehicles run by the asset management titan put down $1.63 billion for Camden Property Trust’s 11-property portfolio. The portfolio is 96 percent occupied, with 3,620 apartment units in Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside and San Diego counties. JLL Capital Markets announced the deal Wednesday after it represented Houston-based Camden in the sale, and arranged $566.6 million in agency acquisition financing for the buyer. The financing covers seven of the properties and consists of a five-year, fixed-rate, interest-only loan structured to allow each asset to be sold or refinanced independently. JLL said the deal is one of the biggest apartment portfolio deals ever completed in Southern California, and that the assets represent roughly 16.5 percent of the region’s average annual multifamily transaction volume by unit count over the past five years. The portfolio includes the Camden, a 287-unit Hollywood development with nearly 39,000 square feet of retail anchored by an Equinox gym; the 380-unit Camden Crown Valley in Mission Viejo; the 469-unit Camden Landmark in Ontario, representing roughly 5 percent of that city’s institutional apartment inventory; and the 132-unit Camden Hillcrest in San Diego, where JLL said no multifamily property with more than 100 units has traded in the past decade. “The significant investor demand for these best-in-class assets in supply-constrained markets underscores the strength of Southern California fundamentals, leading to significant liquidity at scale,” Blake Rogers, senior managing director and multifamily platform leader at JLL, said in a statement. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: BlackRock acquires Camden Property Trust's 11-property SoCal portfolio for $1.63B; 3,620 units, 96% occupied
Properties span LA, Orange, Riverside, San Diego counties; JLL arranged $566.6M agency acquisition financing (5-year, fixed-rate, interest-only)
Largest U.S. multifamily sale since June 2024; portfolio represents ~16.5% of regional supply
stories.summary: BlackRock (via an investment vehicle) acquired Camden Property Trust's 11-property multifamily portfolio in Southern California for $1.63 billion, comprising 3,620 units across Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, and San Diego counties. The portfolio is 96 percent occupied. JLL Capital Markets arranged $566.6 million in agency acquisition financing (five-year, fixed-rate, interest-only loans structured to allow individual asset sales/refinancing). This is the largest U.S. multifamily sale since June 2024 and one of the largest apartment portfolio deals in SoCal history.
stories.impact: Mega-cap institutional multifamily acquisitions in SoCal signal strong portfolio pricing power and investor confidence in regional rent growth and stability despite macro uncertainty; 96% occupancy reinforces tight supply fundamentals. However, large-scale acquisitions by mega-funds (BlackRock) may consolidate ownership, reduce development opportunity sets for smaller operators, and potentially compress cap rates in prime markets—developers should focus on niche, smaller deals and emerging submarkets where institutional capital is less concentrated.
